# Glossary

These are the technical terms and TalentLens-specific names used across *Data Voyage*. Each entry points to the chapter where we teach it or first use it properly. Follow that pointer when a term appears earlier as a forward reference.

---

## TalentLens vocabulary

**Bundled dataset**: The 576-row synthetic corpus shipped with the companion repository, so every chapter runs offline and every quoted number reproduces. Generated by Chapter 5's demo mode (fictional employers, seeded) and cleaned by Chapter 6; `make collect-dataset` gathers real postings with your own Adzuna key. (Chapter 5)

**Canonical schema**: The single row shape every collector maps into: required `title`, `company`, `description`, plus optional salary, location, skills, and source metadata. Chapter 5's `SCHEMA` dict in code is the authority; Chapter 4's table is the reading copy. (Chapter 4)

**Demo vs live collection**: Demo mode generates seeded synthetic postings for reproducibility; live mode calls the Adzuna and RemoteOK APIs with your keys. Numbers in the book come from demo mode; live runs will differ. (Chapter 5)

**jobs_clean.csv**: The cleaned posting file Chapters 6–7 produce under `data/clean/`. Downstream ML, RAG, API, and career scripts read this path via `jobs_clean_path()`. (Chapter 6)

**jobs_raw.csv**: The raw collected file Chapter 5 writes under `data/raw/`. Cleaning is a separate step so you can re-run Chapter 6 without re-fetching. (Chapter 5)

**Role taxonomy**: The five supervised labels TalentLens uses: Data Analyst (DA), Data Scientist (DS), Data Engineer (DE), ML Engineer (MLE), and AI Engineer (AIE). Chapter 6 derives initial `role_category` from title keywords; Chapter 9 learns from body text. (Chapter 1)

**salary_band**: Ordinal bins on annual pay: junior (≤₹8L), mid (₹8–15L), senior (₹15–30L), lead_plus (>₹30L), derived from `salary_min`. Used for EDA charts. Because it is built from pay, it must not be used as a control in tests about pay. (Chapter 6)

**salary_disclosed**: Boolean flag, the posting had employer-supplied salary fields before imputation. Chapter 8 uses it to test whether remote jobs disclose pay more often. (Chapter 6)

**Signposts**: Three optional box labels: **Reference** (lookup tables to skim), **Skip ahead if…** (an expert fast-path), and **Deeper** (optional detail). (Preface)

---

## A

**ADF (Augmented Dickey-Fuller test)**: A unit-root test: if the series is non-stationary, differencing or detrending is required before ARIMA or honest forecasting. (Chapter 14)

**Agent loop**: An explicit cycle of LLM call → parse tool request → execute tool → feed result back until the model returns a final answer. TalentLens implements this in plain Python without a framework wrapper. (Chapter 18)

**ARIMA**: AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average, a classical forecaster for univariate series. We use it after checking stationarity because it forces you to see trend and seasonality instead of hiding them. (Chapter 14)

**ASGI**: Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface, the Python standard FastAPI and uvicorn use so one worker can await I/O (LLM calls, remote embeddings) without blocking the whole process. (Chapter 19)

**A/B testing**: Comparing two variants on live or sampled traffic with a pre-declared metric and stopping rule. Chapter 8's hypothesis tests are the offline analogue for salary and disclosure questions. (Chapter 8)

---

## B

**Bias-variance tradeoff**: Simple models underfit (high bias); complex models overfit training noise (high variance). We pick the simplest model that wins on cross-validated F1, not the fanciest one available. (Chapter 9)

**Bonferroni correction**: When running multiple hypothesis tests, divide α by the number of tests so the family-wise false-positive rate stays controlled. Conservative but appropriate for a small confirmatory battery. (Chapter 8)

**Bundled sample**: See **Bundled dataset** under TalentLens vocabulary.

---

## C

**Chunking**: Splitting long text into overlapping segments before embedding, because sentence-transformer models cap input length. We store multiple chunks per job and score by the best-matching chunk. (Chapter 16)

**Confidence interval**: A range around a sample statistic that quantifies uncertainty. Chapter 3 previews it on synthetic salaries; Chapter 8 uses it with real TalentLens features. (Chapter 3)

**Confusion matrix**: A table of predicted vs actual classes. Off-diagonal cells show which roles we confuse, essential before trusting headline accuracy. (Chapter 9)

**Concurrency group**: A GitHub Actions setting that cancels an in-flight workflow run when a newer push arrives on the same branch, preventing racing deploys. (Chapter 21)

**Cosine similarity**: Measures the angle between two embedding vectors; 1.0 means identical direction, 0 means orthogonal. We use it for semantic job–query matching in vector search. (Chapter 16)

**Cross-validation**: Splitting data into K folds, training K times, and averaging scores so one lucky split cannot fool you. We report mean ± std of macro F1. (Chapter 9)

---

## D

**Dask**: Parallel pandas-like execution across cores or machines. Worth it when data exceeds comfortable RAM; overhead makes it a poor first choice under ~1GB. (Chapter 15)

**Data leakage**: Letting information from the target, the test set, or the future into training features. TalentLens meets it three ways: training on `title` when labels came from `title` (Chapter 9), role-name phrases left in descriptions (Chapter 9), and salaries imputed from the role's median then used to predict role (Chapter 10). (Chapter 6)

**Dropout**: A regulariser for neural networks: during training, randomly zero a fraction of activations so no unit relies on another. Switched off at prediction time with `model.eval()`. (Chapter 12)

---

## E

**Early stopping**: Stop training when validation loss hasn't improved for a set number of epochs, and keep the weights from the best epoch. (Chapter 12)

**Embedding**: A dense numeric vector that encodes text meaning so semantically similar phrases sit close together. We generate them with sentence-transformers for search and skill matching. (Chapter 16)

**EntityRuler**: A spaCy component that matches phrase patterns from a curated skill list, faster and more controllable than training a custom NER model for our glossary. (Chapter 13)

**ESOP (Employee Stock Ownership Plan)**: Equity compensation alongside base salary. In Indian negotiations, ESOPs often move when base is fixed, worth asking even when the first offer looks final. (Chapter 24)

---

## F

**F1 score (macro)**: Harmonic mean of precision and recall, averaged across classes without weighting by frequency. Our primary classifier metric when roles are imbalanced. (Chapter 9)

**FAISS**: Facebook AI Similarity Search, a library for fast approximate nearest-neighbour search over embedding vectors at scale. (Chapter 16)

**False discovery rate (FDR)**: Benjamini–Hochberg procedure: bounds the expected fraction of false positives among rejected nulls. More power than Bonferroni when screening many comparisons. (Chapter 8)

**Feedforward neural network**: Stacked linear layers with non-linear activations between them, mapping inputs to outputs. Chapter 12 measures when one beats a linear baseline and when it only ties. (Chapter 12)

---

## H

**Health check**: A lightweight HTTP endpoint (here `/health`) the platform pings before routing traffic. Must be fast and side-effect free, not a full database query dressed up as liveness. (Chapter 19)

**hnsw**: Hierarchical Navigable Small World, an approximate vector index that trades a small accuracy cost for much faster queries at scale. (Chapter 16)

**Hybrid search**: Combining keyword overlap with vector similarity so exact tech terms and paraphrases both rank well. TalentLens blends the two scores with a weight; Reciprocal Rank Fusion is the common alternative. (Chapter 16)

---

## I

**IDF (inverse document frequency)**: Down-weights words that appear in almost every posting so rare discriminative terms drive TF-IDF features. (Chapter 9)

**Imputation**: Filling missing values with an explicit rule and flag column (`salary_imputed`) so downstream chapters know what was guessed. (Chapter 6)

**IQR (interquartile range)**: Q3 minus Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of salaries, resistant to outliers. We prefer it over standard deviation on skewed pay. (Chapter 3)

**ivfflat**: An approximate vector index that clusters embeddings into lists and searches nearby lists only. Faster builds than hnsw; tune `lists` and `probes` for quality. (Chapter 16)

---

## K

**KMeans**: Partitions unlabeled points into K clusters by minimising within-cluster distance. We choose K using the elbow and silhouette, not silhouette alone. (Chapter 11)

**KPSS test**: Complements ADF: tests the null of stationarity. Disagreement between ADF and KPSS means the series needs careful preprocessing. (Chapter 14)

---

## L

**Layer caching**: Docker reuses unchanged image layers. Copy `requirements*.txt` and install dependencies before copying application code so code edits do not invalidate the pip layer. (Chapter 20)

**log1p transform**: `log(1 + x)` on salaries: compresses the right tail so means, correlations, and plots behave more honestly. Safe at zero salary. (Chapter 3)

**Logistic regression**: Linear classifier on TF-IDF features with softmax over role labels. Often beats heavier models on sparse text at modest data sizes. (Chapter 9)

---

## M

**Mann-Whitney U test**: Nonparametric two-sample test on salaries (or other skewed continuous outcomes) without assuming normality. (Chapter 8)

**Matrix build**: Running the same test job across multiple Python versions in CI to catch version-specific breakage before deploy. (Chapter 21)

**MCAR / MAR / MNAR**: Missing-data mechanisms: Missing Completely At Random, Missing At Random, Missing Not At Random. The mechanism decides whether simple imputation is honest. (Chapter 6)

**Mutual information**: Measures how much knowing a feature reduces uncertainty about the target. We use it for feature selection with a variance gate and noise threshold. (Chapter 10)

---

## O

**One-standard-error rule**: When comparing models by cross-validation, pick the simplest one whose mean score is within one standard deviation of the best. Differences smaller than fold-to-fold noise are not evidence. (Chapter 9)

**OpenAPI**: Machine-readable HTTP API schema FastAPI generates from Pydantic models at `/openapi.json` and `/docs`. (Chapter 19)

**Optional dependencies**: Extra install groups in `pyproject.toml` (`ml`, `llm`, `vectors`) so readers install heavy stacks only when a chapter needs them. (Chapter 2)

**Overfitting**: The model fits training noise: training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises. Stop at the best validation epoch, not the last one. (Chapter 12)

---

## P

**p-hacking**: Running many tests until one crosses α, then reporting only that test. We pre-declare a primary comparison and discuss multiplicity adjustments for the rest. (Chapter 8)

**pgvector**: PostgreSQL extension storing embedding vectors and supporting cosine-distance operators for production RAG backends. (Chapter 16)

**Pipeline (scikit-learn)**: Chains preprocessing and model so the vectoriser fits only on training folds, the standard fix for TF-IDF leakage. (Chapter 9)

**Polars**: Columnar DataFrame engine, often much faster than pandas on large scans. Benchmark it on your own workload before believing any speedup figure. (Chapter 15)

**Precision**: Of everything we predicted as class X, what fraction truly was X. High precision means few false alarms. (Chapter 9)

**Prophet**: Facebook's additive forecasting library with strong seasonality defaults. Named as an alternative; Chapter 14 teaches ARIMA first so assumptions stay visible. (Chapter 14)

**Pydantic**: Validates settings and API request/response shapes at runtime with typed Python models. (Chapter 2)

---

## R

**RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)**: Retrieve relevant documents first, then condition an LLM on that context so answers cite real postings instead of hallucinating listings. (Chapter 16)

**Rate limiting**: Caps requests per time window to protect capacity. Not authentication; identity is a separate layer. (Chapter 19)

**Recall**: Of all true class-X postings, what fraction we found. High recall means few missed roles. (Chapter 9)

**recall@k**: Fraction of relevant jobs appearing in the top-k search results. We plot it to separate ranking noise from retrieval failure. (Chapter 16)

**Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)**: Merges ranked lists by summing `1 / (k + rank)` across keyword and vector results without normalising incompatible scores. (Chapter 16)

---

## S

**sdist**: Source distribution archive (`tar.gz`) published alongside wheels for packages that need to build from source. (Chapter 22)

**Seasonal decomposition**: Splitting a time series into trend, a repeating seasonal pattern of known period, and residual. The period comes from domain knowledge: 7 for daily data with weekly cycles. (Chapter 14)

**Semantic versioning (semver)**: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`: breaking changes bump major, backward-compatible features bump minor, fixes bump patch. (Chapter 22)

**Silhouette score**: Cluster quality metric in [-1, 1]: higher means tighter, well-separated clusters. Favours large K, so use with the elbow, not alone. (Chapter 11)

**SMOTE**: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique: interpolates new minority-class examples for imbalanced tabular data. Named in interview prep; we default to `class_weight='balanced'` first. (Chapter 9)

**SPDX license expression**: Standard string for package licenses (`MIT`, `Apache-2.0`) in `pyproject.toml`. (Chapter 22)

**Standardisation (scaling)**: Rescaling each feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, fitted on training rows only. Essential for neural networks and distance-based methods; irrelevant to trees. (Chapter 12)

**Statistical power**: Probability of detecting a real effect of a given size. Underpowered stratified bins can show "no gap" when the sample is simply too small. (Chapter 8)

**Stratification**: Testing within groups so comparisons stay like-for-like; in Chapter 8, within seniority levels read from job titles. The grouping variable must not be derived from the outcome. (Chapter 8)

---

## T

**TF-IDF**: Term frequency × inverse document frequency sparse text features. Strong baseline for role classification and clustering on job postings. (Chapter 9)

**tiktoken**: Tokeniser library for estimating LLM prompt length; approximate for Llama via Groq but good enough for budget planning. (Chapter 17)

**Tokenization**: Splitting text into tokens (words or subwords) before NLP features. spaCy tokenization respects linguistic boundaries better than naive splits. (Chapter 13)

**Tool calling**: LLM returns structured function invocations (search, fetch detail) instead of free text; the runtime executes them and returns results. (Chapter 18)

**Trusted publishing**: PyPI mechanism letting GitHub Actions publish with short-lived OIDC tokens instead of long-lived API passwords. (Chapter 22)

---

## V

**Vector index**: Data structure (exact scan, ivfflat, or hnsw) that avoids comparing every query embedding to every stored embedding. (Chapter 16)

---

## W

**Wheel**: Built distribution format (`.whl`) pip installs without compiling. Preferred publish artefact on PyPI. (Chapter 22)

**WSGI**: Synchronous Python web gateway interface. Fine for simple apps; ML APIs that await remote models benefit from ASGI instead. (Chapter 19)
